DEF03.title: Building effective agents
DEF03.bibliographic_citation: Erik S. and Barry Zhang. Building effective agents. Anthropic Engineering, December 19, 2024. Live article reviewed October 17, 2026.
DEF03.type: Official practitioner architecture account by the system maintainers
DEF03.paraphrased_definition: Their engineering terminology places both workflows and agents under agentic systems. Workflow control follows predefined code paths; an agent lets the LLM direct its process and tool use. They acknowledge multiple meanings of agent.
DEF03.caveat: Present this as an attributed architectural convention. Their workflows can include model-based routing, dynamic worker decomposition and refinement loops, so conditional edges or a loop are not sufficient tests for agency.
DEF03.version_note: The live page now warns that tooling has changed since the original publication. Use its conceptual distinction, not its present SDK list as a claim about the 2024 implementation.
DEF03.location: What are agents?; Agents; Workflow: Routing; Workflow: Orchestrator-workers; Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer

DEF02.title: Intelligent agents: theory and practice
DEF02.bibliographic_citation: Wooldridge, Michael, and Nicholas R. Jennings. Intelligent agents: theory and practice. The Knowledge Engineering Review 10, no. 2 (June 1995): 115-152. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0269888900008122.
DEF02.type: Primary theoretical/architectural research review by the authors
DEF02.version_note: The author-hosted HTML is an earlier draft stamped November 1994. Use the final 1995 PDF for the bibliographic citation; the HTML makes the definition sections searchable. The final PDF is image-based in the web extractor, so section locators are safer than an unverified PDF page number.
locators: Section 1.1.1, A Weak Notion of Agency
DEF02.paraphrased_definition: Their weak notion groups autonomy, interaction with others, timely response to environmental changes, and goal-directed initiative. A stronger usage additionally invokes mental-state concepts. They explicitly discuss the absence of one universally accepted definition.
DEF02.teaching_use: Use the four properties as questions about behavior, not a modern vendor certification checklist.
DEF02.caveat: These are the authors' historical conceptual distinctions. Neither multiple LLM roles nor a tool-calling interface alone demonstrates all four properties.
DEF02.location: Section 1.1, What is an Agent?; Section 1.1.1, A Weak Notion of Agency

DEF01.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Chapter 2: Intelligent Agents
DEF01.bibliographic_citation: Russell, Stuart J., and Peter Norvig. Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach. 2nd ed. Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall, 2003. Chapter 2, Intelligent Agents, pp. 32-58. Author-hosted chapter draft dated 2002.
DEF01.type: Canonical authored textbook; primary exposition of its agent framework
DEF01.version_note: Despite its current /4th-ed/ URL, the verified sample chapter is the older chapter with printed pages 32-58 and 2002 directory timestamp. Do not cite this PDF as fourth-edition text. The official second-edition page identifies the edition and Prentice Hall; the final book citation is 2003.
DEF01.paraphrased_definition: An agent is viewed through its interaction with an environment: it receives percepts and produces actions. An agent function describes the mapping from percept history to action, while a program implements it. The text treats agency as an analytical viewpoint rather than an absolute classification.
DEF01.teaching_use: Establish the broad historical concept before introducing LLM control loops. Software files, messages and tool results can form the environment; a physical robot is unnecessary.
DEF01.caveat: Rationality is defined relative to evidence and a performance measure; it is not guaranteed success. This broad definition alone does not distinguish a modern LLM agent from ordinary software.
DEF01.location: Section 2.1, printed pp. 32-34 / PDF pp. 1-3; Figure 2.1, printed p. 33 / PDF p. 2; Section 2.2, printed pp. 35-37 / PDF pp. 4-6
DEF01.publisher: Prentice Hall, second edition, Chapter 2, pp. 32–58

DEF04.title: LangGraph overview
DEF04.author: LangChain maintainers
DEF04.bibliographic_citation: LangChain maintainers. LangGraph overview and Tools. Docs by LangChain, Python open-source documentation. Accessed October 17, 2026.
DEF04.type: Official framework and tool-interface documentation; two pages in one documentation collection
locators: LangGraph overview: opening paragraphs and product-role list
Tools: opening definition and Basic tool definition
DEF04.paraphrased_definition: LangGraph is an orchestration framework/runtime for stateful execution, combining programmed and model-driven steps. A tool exposes a callable function through defined inputs and outputs; its description and schema guide invocation.
DEF04.teaching_use: Separate orchestration from decision policy and numerical computation. The same runtime can execute a fixed process or an LLM-directed loop.
DEF04.caveat: A framework's capabilities do not prove that a particular application uses them. A tool is an interface role and may wrap a complex service or another agent. Do not universally equate tool with a trivial or stateless function.
DEF04.location: LangGraph overview: opening paragraphs and product-role list; Tools: opening definition and Basic tool definition
